agent_notes: עֵדֵי חָמָס: construct chain, 'witnesses of violence'. The KJV 'false witnesses' interprets the chamas as perjury; the Hebrew word is wider (violence, injustice). Also 'ask me' is a legal interrogation (cross-questioning), not a charge; the KJV 'laid to my charge' is an interpretive paraphrase. The Radak reading about a demand for money is his own inference ('we do not find this in Samuel') so I mention it as such.

שְׁכוֹל is the noun 'bereavement'; STEPBible 'bereavement', ASV 'bereaving'. KJV 'spoiling' is not supported by the Hebrew; Metzudat Zion and Metzudat David read it as death. I translated as bereavement and noted the interpretations.

'Upon my bosom it returns' is ambiguous. Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David read it as the speaker's prayer for his enemies' good coming back on himself if it was insincere; Ibn Ezra cites R. Levi for a bowed-down posture of prayer; Meiri adds that he prays again and again. I kept the Hebrew ambiguity in the literal layer and leaned toward the 'returns to me' reading in the dramatic layer, without adding a motive.

נֵכִים is a hapax-like and uncertain word. Rashi and Metzudat Zion take it as 'lame, struck in the foot'; Radak as 'abject, struck down' (Job 30:8); Ibn Ezra as 'smitten in spirit'. The five English versions split between 'abjects', 'smiters' and 'low persons'. I chose 'the smitten' in both layers rather than 'the lame', since the sense is disputed; it is also the STEPBible gloss.

קָרְעוּ וְלֹא דָמּוּ: 'tore' (flesh or garments, slander as tearing) and 'did not fall silent' (from דמם) are both in the commentaries; Radak and Metzudat Zion also take קרע as 'opened wide (the mouth)'. I kept the bare verbs literal and explained the options in the commentary.

agent_notes: מָעוֹג is the crux of the psalm. It occurs elsewhere only in 1 Kings 17:12 ('a cake of bread', the widow of Zarephath), which Rashi and Metzudat Zion cite; Radak also records the reading 'idle talk' via Sanhedrin 101b. KJV 'feasts' is an interpretation. I translate 'cake' literally and say in the commentary that the phrase probably means parasite-mockers who laugh for a morsel, as Rashi reads it. The claim about Elijah's widow is an intertext of this corpus; the psalm gives no sign that it alludes to the story.

Gloss for יְחִידָתִי: STEPBible has 'only [life]'. I glossed 'my only one', as Radak ('my soul', after Ps 22:21) and Metzudat Zion ('my soul') read it. KJV 'darling' is archaic and does not render 'only one'.

Reviewer request taken: the second colon now shows the carried-over negative, '[let them not] wink an eye', and pos 8 is glossed '[let them not] wink'. The negative comes from אַל in colon 1 (Metzudat David on Ps 35:19). YLT reads the colon as a plain statement ('wink the eye'); I follow KJV, ASV and Webster in the jussive because יִקְרְצוּ is short-form-compatible and the verse is a prayer.

שֶׁקֶר is taken with 'my enemies' (enemies of falsehood, i.e. without just cause), as Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak read it, not as an adverb of 'rejoice'. KJV 'wrongfully' attaches it to the verb. The sense is close, but the Hebrew word order ties it to the noun. I did not render a possessive 'liars'.

I followed KJV/most moderns in the literal layer: 'the quiet of the land'. Radak himself rejects the 'cleft' reading.

Reviewer request taken: the literal now reads 'our eyes, it has seen' and pos 8 is glossed 'our eyes', so the mismatch between the dual feminine plural noun and the feminine singular verb shows. Commentary reworded to match: KJV and ASV 'our eye hath seen it' make it singular and add 'it'; BBE alone has 'eyes ... have seen it'.

עֵינֵינוּ is dual in form (עֵינַיִם, construct עֵינֵי) with a 1cp suffix. A feminine singular verb with a dual or plural subject is ordinary Hebrew grammar, so I do not treat it as an error or a textual problem, only as something the literal layer should keep visible.

agent_notes: The packet gives deity.yhwh as the entity for אֲדֹנָי and אֱלֹהַי as well as יהוה. I glossed אֲדֹנָי as 'O Lord' and kept YHWH only for the tetragrammaton.

הָעִירָה and הָקִיצָה are -āh lengthened imperatives (cohortative-shaped, with the emphatic ending), not feminine. Malbim's reading (wake the dead witnesses whom the enemies cited) is his own homiletic extension, mentioned in the commentary only as his.

Five versions split on נַפְשֵׁנוּ. KJV/ASV/Webster 'so would we have it' and BBE 'so we will have it' paraphrase; YLT keeps 'our desire'. I took nefesh as 'our appetite/desire' and kept the throat nuance (the same word means 'throat') for the commentary only, since the next clause is 'we have swallowed him'. The gloss corrects STEPBible 'desire our' to 'our desire', since the Hebrew has no verb.
אַל + imperfect (jussive) is a wish ('let them not say'); YLT renders it as a plain statement. I follow the jussive reading, which is also Radak's and Targum's.

history.note: [consider] Attribute the throat sense to yourself, and give Radak's and Metzudat David's 'our soul is glad' as theirs. (Radak on PS.35.25: "האח נפשנו כלומר שמחנו נפשנו"; Metzudat David: "שמחה נפשנו")

agent_notes: The packet's Ibn Ezra comment on this verse (that 'together' answers 'the smiters gathered against me', v.15, and a remark on the verb 'magnify') is clipped and I could not read the second half with confidence, so I do not cite him here. The 'together' pairing with v.15 is Radak's point as well, and I rely on Radak.
Meiri reads 'his servant' as the whole nation (as in 'Jacob my servant'), Radak as David. I mention both and do not choose.

צִדְקִי 'my righteousness' can mean my vindication or my just cause (Radak: what is right and due to me). 'My vindication' in the dramatic layer is my reading; the literal layer keeps 'my righteousness'.

Hebrew סְגֹר is disputed: 'close/bar [the way]' (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Metzudat David) or a noun for a weapon, 'javelin/battle-axe' (Radak reports that some take it as the name of a weapon; the Targum reads a verb, 'slam shut'). The KJV 'stop the way' follows the first. I chose 'close off', hedged in the commentary. STEPBible 'lance' reflects the weapon reading and was corrected.
STEPBible glosses לִקְרַאת as 'to meet'; kept literally 'to meet' in the literal layer, since the idiom is hostile or friendly by context.

agent_notes: שַׁחַת רִשְׁתָּם is a construct chain, but its sense is disputed: 'their net [in] a pit' (KJV), 'pit of their net' (Radak's reading as a pit covered with a net), or two separate nouns (Metzudat Zion, Meiri's alternative). The pit's wording is repeated through the verse; I kept the chain literally. The ambiguity of the second חִנָּם (modifying 'dug' vs. the whole line) is the reason the literal layer repeats 'without cause'.

Singular 'him' after plural enemies in vv.7-8: Radak takes it distributively (each enemy) or of Saul; Meiri similarly. I rendered 'him' literally. KJV and BBE differ (BBE pluralizes). Also שׁוֹאָה: 'ruin/storm' in standard lexica; Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it as 'darkness' (cf. Job 30:3), which I mention but do not adopt.
Gloss for תִּלְכְּדוֹ: STEPBible 'may it catch him' with the net as subject. The net is feminine (רֶשֶׁת), so the verb is feminine; I translated accordingly.
